title: Stop AI Agent Hallucinations: 5 Techniques + Production Patterns - Elizabeth Fuentes, AWS

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is the agent system—its loops, multi-agent Swarm patterns, lifecycle-hook control plane, and steering mechanisms for preventing hallucinations through architectural code changes rather than prompt tweaks. Techniques are general-purpose agent architecture patterns demonstrated via a travel agent, with production deployment on Amazon Bedrock Agent Core as a developer platform. The workshop covers building agents locally, evaluating against 90 ground-truth queries with before/after metrics, and deploying to production via Amazon Bedrock Agent Core with live rule updates. Requires Python, agent frameworks, vector search, Neo4j/Cypher, and AWS familiarity to follow the hands-on demos. Hands-on workshop with live code demos, side-by-side comparisons, and repository walkthrough. All cited evidence is directly stated in the transcript with character-level anchors.

summary: Elizabeth Fuentes presents five architectural techniques to stop AI agent hallucinations, emphasizing that each is a code change, not a prompt change. The core problem is that agents hallucinate when too much, too little, or irrelevant information enters context—and every token costs money. The demo environment is a travel agent built with Strands, an AWS open-source agent framework, using OpenAI as model provider, sentence transformers for local embeddings, FAISS as a local vector store, and Neo4j for graph RAG. Technique 1 (semantic tool selection) filters 29 tools to the top 3 relevant ones per query using vector search, reducing tool-description tokens from ~3,000 to under 300 per call. A swap_tools function in Strands' agentic loop clears and re-adds tools per invocation for conversation scenarios. Production deployment uses Amazon Bedrock Agent Core Gateway, which handles tool indexing and routing automatically. Technique 2 (GraphRAG) addresses vector-search RAG's inability to aggregate, count, or traverse relationships across the full dataset. GraphRAG uses Neo4j to build a knowledge graph from documents; the model writes Cypher queries that run across all data and return computed, verified results—including honest zero-results answers. Neo4j's library can auto-build the knowledge graph from raw text using an LLM. Technique 3 (multi-agent validation) addresses the problem of single agents hiding tool errors behind confident success responses. The solution uses Strands' built-in Swarm class to chain executor, validator, and critic agents with automatic handoff. Technique 4 (neuro-symbolic guardrails) addresses the limitation that rules written in system prompts or tool descriptions are treated as suggestions, not constraints. Only code executes logic. Strands provides lifecycle hooks (hook_provider, hook_register, before_to_call_event) that fire before tool execution, intercepting calls and checking parameters against coded rules. Demonstrated rules include date validation, maximum 10 guests per booking, payment required before confirmation, and cancellation within 48 hours. Hooks are all-or-nothing—unconditional block or approve. Technique 5 (agent steering) addresses soft constraints where hard hooks would force user retry unnecessarily. Using the agent control library, rules are registered on a local server via API and the agent picks them up without code changes. The steering agent self-corrects: booking 50 guests results in splitting the reservation into two rooms rather than blocking. The final module shows production deployment via Amazon Bedrock Agent Core, providing a managed runtime, gateway (routing tool calls to Lambda functions automatically), short-term and long-term memory, CloudWatch observability, and no servers to manage. Production rules can be changed live in DynamoDB without redeployment. Neo4j AuraDB offers an external graph database with a free tier. Two deployment options are available in the repository: notebook-based or CDK (Cloud Development Kit). AWS credits are provided in the resource links. Elizabeth encourages developers to progress from demo 1 through demo 5 and then deploy to production with Amazon Bedrock Agent Core, with all demos available as both notebooks and applications in the open-source repository.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agent hallucinations are architectural, not prompt-engineering, failures—fixing them requires code-level changes.
Semantic tool selection filters 29 tools to 3 relevant ones via vector search, cutting tool-description tokens from ~3,000 to under 300 per call.
Vector-search RAG cannot aggregate, count, or traverse relationships across a full dataset—GraphRAG with Neo4j returns computed, verified results via Cypher queries instead.
Multi-agent validation with Strands Swarm chains executor, validator, and critic agents so fabricated successes are caught and surfaced as clear failures to the user.
Rules in prompts are suggestions; only code executes logic—neuro-symbolic guardrails use Strands lifecycle hooks to intercept tool calls before execution and enforce hard constraints.
Agent steering uses soft constraints via a local server (agent control library) so agents self-correct instead of blocking—e.g., splitting 50 guests across two rooms.
Amazon Bedrock Agent Core provides managed production deployment: runtime, gateway, memory, and observability with no servers to manage.
Production rules can be changed live in DynamoDB without redeployment; Neo4j AuraDB provides a free-tier external graph database option.
The open-source repository contains all demos as notebooks and applications, plus CDK and notebook-based deployment options, with AWS credits in the resource links.
Elizabeth recommends progressing from demo 1 through demo 5, then deploying to production with Amazon Bedrock Agent Core.

sections.title: Introduction: Five Techniques Beyond the Prompt
sections.summary: Elizabeth introduces the five techniques to stop agent hallucinations: semantic tool selection, graph RAG, multi-agent validation, neuro-symbolic guardrails, and runtime guardrails. Each is a code change, not a prompt change. The core problem: paying for tokens that are too much, too little, or missing important information, causing hallucinations.

sections.title: Speaker Intro and Demo Setup
sections.summary: Elizabeth Fuentes, AWS developer advocate focused on agentic applications, introduces herself. The demo uses a travel agent built with Strands, an open-source agent framework maintained by AWS. A QR code links to all code and resources.

sections.title: Semantic Tool Selection: The Problem
sections.summary: The travel agent has 29 tools (flights, hotels, payments, weather, cancellations). On every call, all 29 tool schemas go into context. Each schema costs 17-200 tokens, totaling ~3,000 tokens per call just for tool descriptions, whether or not tools are used.

sections.title: Semantic Tool Selection: Code Setup and Requirements
sections.summary: Demo setup in Jupyter notebook: installing Strands agent, OpenAI API, sentence transformers for local embeddings, FAISS vector store, Neo4j. Elizabeth shows 29 dummy tools and explains the semantic index building process.

sections.title: Semantic Tool Selection: Baseline vs Semantic Approach Demo
sections.summary: Baseline agent with all 29 tools spends ~2,000 tokens per question with suboptimal accuracy across 90 queries. Semantic approach sends each query to vector search first, retrieves top 3 relevant tools, and only sends those to the model. Results show large token reduction and improved accuracy.

sections.title: Semantic Tool Selection: Conversation Scenario and Swap Tools
sections.summary: For conversation scenarios with memory, tools must be swapped in and out per invocation using Strands agentic loop to avoid re-accumulating all 29 tools. The swap_tools function clears tools and adds new relevant ones each turn.

sections.title: Production Deployment with Amazon Bedrock Agent Core Gateway
sections.summary: For production, Amazon Bedrock Agent Core Gateway builds the tool index and handles vector search and tool routing automatically. Developers register tools once and the gateway finds the right one for each request.

sections.title: GraphRAG: Problem and Concept
sections.summary: Vector-search RAG works for open-ended questions but breaks down for aggregation, counting, and relationship traversal. Vector search returns top-N chunks and the model estimates from that sample, presenting estimates as facts. GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from documents; the model writes Cypher queries that run across all data and return computed, verified results.

sections.title: GraphRAG: Demo Setup
sections.summary: Demo setup: OpenAI for model, Neo4j locally for graph RAG, simple file-based vector store for traditional RAG, sentence transformers for embeddings. Two engines are created side by side—a RAG engine using the vector store and a graph engine using Neo4j. The graph tool requires the model to write a Cypher query, which is placed in context.

sections.title: GraphRAG: Side-by-Side Comparison Results
sections.summary: Four question types compared: aggregation, counting, room types/prices, and non-existent data. RAG estimates or hedges; Graph returns precise, honest answers including zero-results for non-existent data (e.g., no hotels in Antarctica).

sections.title: GraphRAG: Neo4j Knowledge Graph Auto-Building
sections.summary: Neo4j's library can auto-build the knowledge graph from raw text data using an LLM. Developers send text files to the library, which understands the data and constructs the graph automatically—no manual graph creation needed.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Validation: Problem and Concept
sections.summary: A single agent that calls a tool and gets an error will rationalize the error and return a confident success response—the user never sees the error. The solution is a validation layer with three agents in sequence: one acts, one checks, and one approves or rejects. Strands has a built-in Swarm class that manages handoff between agents automatically.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Validation: Swarm Demo
sections.summary: Demo creates three agents—executor, validator, and critic—chained via Swarm. Test scenarios validate hotel bookings: valid hotel (expect true), non-existing hotel (expect false), missing booking (expect false). The live demo showed the swarm flow working after resolving technical hiccups.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Validation: Swarm vs Single Agent Comparison
sections.summary: The single agent returns success for non-existent bookings, while the swarm's executor gets the error, the validator catches it, and the critic rejects it—the user sees a clear failure instead of a fabricated confirmation. Comparison output shows the single agent saying everything is correct while the swarm flags the missing issue.

sections.title: Neuro-Symbolic Guardrails: Problem and Concept
sections.summary: Rules written in system prompts or tool descriptions are read as suggestions, not constraints—the model processes them as probabilistic text, not logic. Only code executes logic. A rule in the prompt may be followed or ignored; a rule in code cannot be escaped. Strands provides lifecycle hooks (hook_provider, hook_register, before_to_call_event) that fire at specific moments in the agent loop—specifically right before a tool executes—intercepting the call and checking parameters.

sections.title: Neuro-Symbolic Guardrails: Code Setup
sections.summary: Demo setup requires only Strands and OpenAI. The Strands base class provides hook_provider, hook_register, and before_to_call_event. The before_to_call event fires every time the model is about to execute a tool, making it possible to intercept the call before it runs. An after_to_call event also exists but is not used in this demo.

sections.title: Neuro-Symbolic Guardrails: Rules and Hooks Implementation
sections.summary: Business rules are defined in Python: validate dates (check-in before check-out), maximum 10 guests per booking, payment required before confirmation, cancellation within 48 hours of check-in. Validation hooks are created using hook_provider, and booking rules, confirmation rules, and state are added. The normal engine is only three lines (tools, model); the hooked engine adds the neuro-symbolic hook line.

sections.title: Neuro-Symbolic Guardrails: Side-by-Side Demo Results
sections.summary: Three scenarios compared: confirm booking without payment (normal engine confirms; hooked engine blocks with 'Payment must be verified'), booking exceeding 10-guest limit (normal engine allows 15; hooked engine blocks), and valid booking for 5 guests (both pass all rules). Same model, same tools, same prompt—different outcomes because rules are in Python, not the prompt. Amazon Bedrock Agent Core policies service applies the same concept at a structural level in production.

sections.title: Agent Steering: Soft Constraints vs Hard Hooks
sections.summary: Hooks block unconditionally, stopping the agent and forcing user retry—correct for hard constraints but wrong for soft ones. Soft constraints include a room fitting 4 guests but 6 could book two rooms, or a full flight with availability on the next one. Agent steering lets the agent find an option and complete the task instead of blocking. Rules are registered on a local server via API using the agent control library; the agent picks them up without code changes, unlike hooks which require code changes and redeployment.

sections.title: Agent Steering: Demo
sections.summary: Using the agent control library with two key imports (AIN control plugin for capturing events, AIN control student handle for listening to steering decisions). Booking for 50 guests—exceeding the 10-guest limit—results in the agent splitting the reservation into two rooms (one for 45, one for 5) instead of blocking. The hook blocks hard constraints; agent control handles soft rules.

sections.title: Production Deployment: Amazon Bedrock Agent Core
sections.summary: Everything demonstrated locally runs in production via Amazon Bedrock Agent Core, which provides a managed runtime, gateway (routing tool calls to Lambda functions automatically), short-term and long-term memory, CloudWatch observability, and no servers to manage. The Strands engine runs inside the runtime, and other frameworks can be used as well.

sections.title: Production Deployment Details and Recap
sections.summary: Production rules can be changed live in DynamoDB without redeployment—they update on the next call. Neo4j AuraDB offers an external graph database with a free tier. AWS credentials are needed for Bedrock Agent Core, and AWS credits are available in the resource links. Two deployment options exist in the repository: notebook-based or CDK (Cloud Development Kit). Elizabeth recaps all five techniques: semantic tool selection for token waste, GraphRAG for computed answers instead of sampling, multi-agent validation for fabricated successes, neuro-symbolic guardrails for rules the model cannot skip, and agent steering for self-correction instead of hard blocks. She encourages progressing from demo 1 through demo 5, then deploying to production. All demos are available as notebooks and applications in the repository.

limitations: Demo uses dummy/simulated travel tools, not production-ready
Some queries are intentionally ambiguous with similar tool names, causing occasional wrong picks
Accuracy is not perfect even with semantic filtering due to generic dummy tool names
Conversation scenario increases token usage because chat history is sent with each message
FAISS local vector store is simple; production may need more robust stores
Vector-search RAG fundamentally cannot aggregate, count, or traverse relationships across full datasets

Neuro-symbolic hooks are all-or-nothing blocks—changing a rule requires changing code and redeploying the whole engine
Agent steering demo had live technical issues (model provider errors, commented-out cells)
Agent control library requires running a local server for rule registration
